tasks.label: Select and fasten bulldozer blades or other attachments to tractors, using hitches.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Compact machine attachment swap on an active jobsite: skid-steer/compact track loader operator changes between bucket, pallet forks, auger, breaker or broom. Attachments sit on uneven, often muddy ground in a laydown area; operator picks the right one, drives up, aligns the quick-attach plate, engages the locking levers or hydraulic pins, connects auxiliary hydraulic couplers, and tugs to verify lock.

Excavator or backhoe attachment change on a jobsite using a pin-grabber or fully automatic coupler: swapping a digging bucket for a grading bucket, hydraulic hammer, compactor or thumb. Machine tracks to the attachment lying on grade, curls the coupler onto the pins, engages the lock, connects/pressurizes hydraulic lines, and confirms engagement before working.

Heavy implement mount or removal in the contractor's shop or equipment yard: installing/removing a dozer blade with push arms, a ripper, a loader bucket or counterweight. The multi-ton component is slung by overhead crane or a second machine, pins are aligned and driven, retaining bolts torqued, and cylinders/hydraulic lines reconnected on level, lit, controlled premises.

Hitching towed equipment in the yard or staging area: coupling a trailer, water wagon, roller or compactor to a tractor, truck or dozer using a pintle, ball, gooseneck or fifth-wheel hitch; setting the coupler, safety chains, and brake/light or air lines, on paved, institution-controlled premises.

Bolt-on attachment and mount kits in the shop: fitting a snow plow/wing mount or winch bracket, or replacing bolt-on cutting edges and end bits on a blade or bucket. Heavy parts are positioned, holes lined up, and bolts run down and torqued to spec with impact/torque tools.

Field fit-up and plumbing of a non-standard attachment on the jobsite: routing flexible hydraulic hoses and a wiring harness, threading and wrench-tightening fittings, adding adapters, and zip-tying/clamping lines so the attachment functions on that particular carrier.

tasks.label: Operate loaders to pull out stumps, rip asphalt or concrete, rough-grade properties, bury refuse, or perform general cleanup.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Mass/rough grading of a large open site: operator runs a wheel loader or track loader on a stripped building pad, subdivision, solar/wind, or industrial-park site, pushing and spreading imported fill and cutting/filling to rough subgrade over open ground with no vertical construction yet, working to stakes or a machine-control model.

Rough grading and backfilling on a smaller property/lot: loader works around foundations, curbs, utility trenches, drop inlets and stockpiled materials while carpenters, pipe crews and laborers work nearby; frequent repositioning, spotters, and hand-work interfaces.

Bulk cleanup: loading stockpiled spoil, broken rock and rubble from defined piles into haul trucks, pushing loose material into piles, and cleaning up spilled aggregate in the open areas of an active jobsite.

Detailed cleanup at the end of a job or between trades: picking up scattered mixed debris (broken concrete, timber, rebar, forms, trash, mud) in tight quarters around finished work, dressing up around structures and paved areas without damaging them.

Ripping and removing pavement: loader with ripper tooth or bucket tearing up asphalt or concrete on a road, driveway or parking lot rehab/demolition job, then loading the broken slab material out into trucks.

Land clearing and burial work: grubbing stumps and roots out with the bucket/forks, piling brush after tree removal, and burying refuse or debris in an on-site pit or pushing and covering waste at a landfill working face.

tasks.label: Operate equipment to demolish or remove debris or to remove snow from streets, roads, or parking lots.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Municipal/state DOT snow plowing of public streets and highways with a plow truck or motor grader: night shift, live traffic, parked cars, mailboxes, hidden curbs and manholes, wing plow and spreader control, blowing snow and low visibility.

Contractor clearing a commercial parking lot or private site lot with a wheel loader, skid steer or pickup plow: pushing and stacking snow in designated piles, working around parked vehicles, islands, curbs and pedestrians on premises controlled by the property owner.

Snow removal on a closed institutional property — airport runways/taxiways/aprons or a large industrial or campus roadway network — with big plow/sweeper units, often in coordinated fleets on planned routes under facility control.

Structure demolition with an excavator fitted with hammer, shear, pulverizer or grapple: taking down a building, wall or slab in place, sequencing cuts for stability, wetting dust, working near adjacent structures.

Bulk debris/spoil removal on an open jobsite: excavator or front-end loader digging out broken material and loading haul trucks repetitively, plus dozing spoil into piles, on a site being cleared or graded.

Mixed demolition or storm rubble handling: grappling concrete chunks with rebar, wood, metal and trash from around standing structures or at a disposal/recycling yard, separating and loading into trucks or hoppers.

tasks.label: Adjust handwheels and depress pedals to control attachments, such as blades, buckets, scrapers, or swing booms.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Hydraulic excavator on a large site-prep / heavy-civil jobsite (data center pad, manufacturing plant, highway cut): repetitive bucket, boom and swing control to strip, dig to a design surface, and load articulated haul trucks that shuttle in and out; open terrain, dust, changing bench, crew and trucks nearby.

Motor grader or scraper: handwheel/pedal control of the moldboard or scraper bowl to cut subgrade, crown and slope a roadway, maintain haul roads or fine-grade a pad to tight tolerance, often under traffic control and on material that varies pass to pass.

Wheel loader bucket work at an institution-controlled yard (aggregate pit, ready-mix or asphalt plant, material yard): repetitive V-cycle bucket filling from stockpiles and charging trucks or hoppers, cleaning up the working floor, fixed layout with controlled access.

Foundation/pile work with an excavator-mounted attachment on solar, utility or foundation jobs: positioning the boom over surveyed points and driving steel piles or screw anchors to plumb and z-height tolerance, thousands of repetitions across a site.

tasks.label: Check fuel supplies at sites to ensure adequate availability.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-shift/mid-shift check of the operator's own machine (excavator, dozer, loader, grader) on an active construction site: climb the machine, key on and read the in-cab fuel gauge or open the fuel cap and eyeball/dip the tank, decide whether the machine has enough fuel for the shift and call the fuel truck if not. Mud, dust, cold, uneven ground, other trades working nearby.

End-of-day or start-of-day round of several parked machines on the jobsite: walk from machine to machine, check each fuel level, top off from the on-site fuel truck or skid tank, and record levels/quantities so equipment is ready to run at start of shift. Often done in the dark or after crews leave.

Check the on-site bulk fuel supply (500–1,000 gal cube/skid tank or fuel trailer): read the sight tube or clock gauge or drop a dipstick, check for water/contamination, estimate days of supply against planned production, and call in a delivery. Tank sits in a bermed area or locked cage in a laydown yard that moves as the job progresses.

Check fuel on auxiliary equipment scattered across a linear or roadway project — light towers, generator sets, dewatering pumps, compressors — reading small tank gauges/sight tubes at each unit, often at night, in the right-of-way with live traffic, and topping off from a service truck.

Check the fuel farm / bulk storage at the contractor's equipment yard, quarry, or asphalt plant before dispatching equipment and fuel trucks: read the tank level gauges on the fixed fuel farm, verify the service truck's load, log readings and order resupply. Fixed layout, controlled premises, standard tank installations.

sources.title: SCOTT making ROBOFUEL refuelling system progress with AHS mining truck fleets - International Mining

tasks.label: Drive tractor-trailer trucks to move equipment from site to site.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Lowboy/RGN haul of a large machine (excavator, dozer, motor grader) between two active job sites: back the machine up ramps onto the deck, chain it down with binders, check height/width and oversize permit routing, drive 20-150 miles on interstates and surface streets, then unload on dirt at the receiving site with a spotter.

Short local move of small/medium equipment (skid steer, roller, mini excavator, compressor, light plant) on a tag or deck trailer: load and strap in a cramped staging area, drive city streets in traffic, unload at the curb or in a fenced-off work zone, often several such moves in a day.

Move from the contractor's equipment yard or shop to a job site: load at the yard's ramp or dock, secure the machine and its attachments, run public highways to the site, set the machine off, and deadhead or shuttle back.

Move inside one large gate-controlled site (quarry, mine, industrial plant, or a closed section of a highway project): haul a machine on a lowboy between work areas over internal haul roads, no public traffic, premises controlled by the operator.

Support runs: deadheading the empty lowboy back, or hauling attachments, crane counterweights, mats, fuel/water tanks; includes DOT pre-trip inspection, fueling, permit and route paperwork, and coordinating escorts for oversize loads.

tasks.label: Push other equipment when extra traction or assistance is required.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Push-loading self-propelled scrapers on a mass-grading or highway earthwork job: the dozer operator matches the scraper's speed in the cut, engages the push block cleanly, applies tractive force through the load cycle, then backs out and repeats for a train of scrapers as the cut line moves during the shift.

Recovering a bogged machine on an active site: a loader, articulated truck or another dozer is stuck in mud or soft fill; the operator judges ground conditions and contact/hookup points, sometimes rigging chains or a push bar, and pushes or nudges in coordination with the stuck machine's operator without damaging tracks, counterweights or hydraulics.

Traction assist on grades and soft ground: a dozer pushes loaded off-road trucks, water trucks or a compactor up a wet haul road, a landfill working face, or a steep fill lift, staying in contact under load while the assisted machine's operator manages throttle and steering; repeated over many passes in rain or thaw conditions.

Moving a disabled or non-running machine: pushing a dead roller, skid steer or loader clear of the work area, into a shop bay, or onto a lowboy trailer, in a contractor's equipment yard or laydown area with a fixed layout and controlled access.

Push-assisting a machine performing work or repositioning: e.g., nudging a sheepsfoot compactor or a pile/drill rig into position on a soft pad, or helping a mired lowboy/service truck through a soft haul road on an active jobsite with crew and other equipment nearby.

Transfer to this task fails — pushing a pile of dirt requires no alignment with, contact-force modulation against, or coordination with a second manned machine, which is the essence of push-loading a scraper or freeing a bogged machine.

tasks.label: Operate road watering, oiling, or rolling equipment, or street sealing equipment, such as chip spreaders.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Breakdown/intermediate/finish rolling behind an asphalt paver on a mainline highway lane, arterial, or large open mat (big parking lot, airport-type paving). Long, largely straight passes at controlled speed and temperature inside a coned-off lane, coordinating with the paver and haul trucks; density and smoothness must meet spec.

Rolling asphalt on urban/residential streets and complex geometry: intersections, cul-de-sacs, driveway aprons, tight radii, manholes and valve boxes to roll around, longitudinal joints against existing pavement, hand-work areas with rakers, live traffic and parked cars adjacent, frequent stops and repositioning.

Compacting soil, embankment lifts, subgrade and aggregate base on roadway and site-grading jobs with a padfoot or smooth-drum vibratory roller: repetitive passes over a lift laid by dozers/scrapers, adjusting amplitude and pass count to hit density, working around haul traffic and grade stakes on a changing earthwork site.

Running a water truck/water pull for dust control and moisture conditioning: repeated circuits over haul roads, subgrade and stockpile areas, refilling at a hydrant, pond, or fill station, and metering spray rate/pass count so the surface is damp but not slick or over-watered.

Chip seal / surface treatment work: operating the asphalt distributor (oiling) truck to shoot binder at spec rate and temperature, and the chip spreader hitched to dump trucks, spreading aggregate at the specified rate immediately behind the shot on rural roads and streets, matching joints, protecting driveways and structures, in convoy with rollers and a broom.

Tight-area and patch compaction: small ride-on or walk-behind rollers on utility trench cuts, pavement patches, parking-lot corners and around castings, curbs and utility appurtenances, often on a street shoulder with traffic passing and laborers working alongside.

tasks.label: Operate compactors, scrapers, or rollers to level, compact, or cover refuse at disposal grounds.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Active working face of a large municipal solid waste landfill: operating a wheeled landfill compactor (e.g., Cat 836 / Bomag BC) through a shift to push, spread and compact incoming refuse in thin lifts, making repeated passes to hit density targets while trucks tip, spotters direct traffic, bulky/odd items (mattresses, tires, wire, appliances) appear, and the face slope must be kept safe and uniform.

End-of-day cover: dozer or compactor with blade pushes and grades six inches of soil, or places alternative cover/tarps, over the day's waste on irregular waste slopes, working in fading light, mud or wind, and leaving a drainable, fully covered surface for regulatory compliance.

Hauling and spreading intermediate or final cover soil with scrapers or articulated trucks plus a dozer over completed cells: load or receive borrow soil, haul on temporary landfill roads, dump, spread to a specified thickness and grade to drainage slopes over settling waste.

Roller/compactor work on soil at the disposal ground: compacting cover-soil lifts, cell subgrade or liner protection layers, working pads and haul roads to a specified density over a surveyed, previously graded area.

Small rural municipal or construction-and-demolition disposal site: one operator alternates between a dozer, loader and roller, levelling heterogeneous C&D debris and bulky items, then covering with soil; self-haul public customers and their vehicles are present near the face, and the machines carry little or no positioning instrumentation.

tasks.label: Test atmosphere for adequate oxygen or explosive conditions when working in confined spaces.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-entry atmospheric test of a street or sewer manhole / utility vault on a utility or roadway construction job: operator bump-checks a pumped 4-gas monitor (O2, LEL, CO, H2S), feeds a 15-25 ft sampling hose down the shaft, holds readings at the top, middle and bottom (about 2 minutes per level), and records results on the entry permit before anyone or any equipment goes in. Traffic, weather, unknown vault geometry, water and debris.

Excavation or trench deeper than 4 ft on an active construction site (sewer/water line cut, footing, pit): test the air near the bottom of the cut before workers descend and re-test as the cut deepens or after fuel-burning equipment, adjacent gas mains, landfill or contaminated soil raise risk. Narrow (3-6 ft wide) muddy cut whose geometry changes hourly, spoil piles and machines alongside.

Monitoring during the work rather than before it: a monitor is worn by the entrant or hung/left in the space while a small machine or pump runs, readings are watched continuously, the space is ventilated and re-tested after an alarm, and work is stopped and people pulled out if O2 falls below 19.5% or LEL exceeds 10%. Construction site, changing sources of exhaust and vapor.

Confined-space test inside an institution-controlled facility where the operator is working: wastewater plant wet well or digester, pump station, water tank, plant vault, tunnel heading or mine drift, under a written permit program with fixed layouts, standard access hatches and controlled premises.

Instrument preparation plus degraded/awkward conditions: field zero, bump test and calibration check of the detector at shift start, then testing a partially flooded vault, culvert, shaft or drilled caisson in cold, rain, dust or at a remote site, and documenting the readings for the competent person.

tasks.label: Turn valves to control air or water output of compressors or pumps.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Portable diesel air compressor on an active building/roadway construction site: operator opens/closes the service (ball) valves on the manifold, sets the pressure regulator, bleeds off pressure and cracks valves open to charge hoses feeding pneumatic breakers or drills, adjusting output as tools are added or dropped. Outdoors, mud, dust, cords and hoses on uneven ground; machine placement changes daily.

Dewatering / trash pump at an excavation, trench or footing: operator primes the pump, opens suction and throttles the discharge gate or butterfly valve (stiff, multi-turn handwheels, often muddy) to control water output so the sump is drawn down without losing prime or over-pumping into a settling tank; repeated adjustment as inflow changes and as the pump is relocated.

Water truck / water wagon for dust control and compaction moisture on a haul road or grade: operator works the tank fill valve at a hydrant or pond fill pipe and the spray-bar/cannon valves (cab levers or manual valves) to control water output rate over the surface, varying with speed, wind, and how dry the surface is.

Contractor equipment yard, shop or asphalt/concrete batch plant: operator or operating engineer runs a shop/plant air compressor and water pump — opening supply valves, setting the regulator for air tools and tire inflation, opening wash-down water valves — at fixed, standard piping in a company-controlled, maintained facility.

Established pump station or manifold on a large project (tunnel dewatering, dam or wellpoint system, water treatment tie-in): operator turns valves on a staged pump manifold to bring pumps on line, balance flow between discharge lines and hold a set output, checking pressure and flow gauges; fixed engineered layout with controlled access.

sources.title: Operator | Taurob
sources.claim: Taurob's Operator robot, developed out of the ARGOS/oil-and-gas program, is offered commercially as able to operate autonomously when interacting with plant hardware such as valves and dial gauges, i.e. autonomous valve manipulation inside industrial process facilities.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the same physical action as the task: rotating industrial valve handwheels/levers on process piping (pumps, compressors) and reading the dial gauges that indicate resulting pressure/flow.

sources.title: ADNOC deploys heavy-duty robot at Taweelah Gas Compression Plant | Hydrocarbon Engineering
sources.claim: Taurob's heavy-duty robot is deployed and running autonomous routine rounds inside a live gas compression plant, establishing that the platform navigates and works unattended in a structured industrial facility full of pumps, compressors and valve manifolds.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes autonomous unattended operation of the same platform family in a compression plant (E2 facility); the manipulation variant of this platform is the one credited with valve turning.

sources.title: ATEX-Certified Robots for Oil & Gas: Zone 1 & Zone 2 Inspection in Hazardous Refineries
sources.claim: The Taurob arm is described as enabling physical interaction with plant hardware — turning manual valves and opening ... inspection rounds on live production facilities.

sources.title: Boston Dynamics Expands Spot® Product Line | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' commercially sold Spot Arm performs constrained-motion manipulation including opening and closing valves and pulling levers, via semi-autonomous actions rather than continuous joysticking.
sources.transferJustification: Same action class as the task (rotating valve handles/levers on plant piping); autonomy marked unclear because the product text says semi-autonomous, so this item is treated as supporting only in combination with the autonomous-mission evidence.

sources.system: Spot / Orbit Autowalk missions with Spot Arm
sources.title: The Next Step in Safe, Autonomous Robotic Inspection | Boston Dynamics
sources.claim: Spot's arm manipulation is now executed inside fully autonomous Autowalk inspection missions in customer facilities — the robot opens doors on its own during unattended rounds, and gauge-reading actions are performed automatically in the same missions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous door-handle manipulation is the same constrained-rotation grasp-and-turn problem as turning a valve lever/handwheel, on comparable hardware at comparable precision, inside human work facilities; paired with the same robot's autonomous gauge reading it closes the see-adjust-verify loop this task needs.

sources.title: Team NimbRo at MBZIRC 2017: Autonomous valve stem turning using a wrench - Journal of Field Robotics
sources.claim: A fully autonomous mobile manipulator located a valve panel in a large outdoor arena, selected and grasped a wrench, and turned a valve stem without teleoperation, winning the MBZIRC 2017 challenge.
sources.transferJustification: Same physical operation as the task (perceiving and rotating a valve on a fixed panel); performed in a purpose-built challenge arena, so it anchors the E1 counterfactual where the valve is presented to the machine.

sources.system: Cat 789D Autonomous Water Truck (Command for hauling + automated Water Delivery System)
sources.title: New Cat® 789D Autonomous Water Truck defeats dust and controls costs through automated water delivery
sources.claim: Caterpillar's commercially available 789D Autonomous Water Truck runs unmanned on mine haul roads and automates the water delivery itself, metering spray output over the road surface rather than only driving the truck.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine-controlled actuation of the truck's water valves/spray heads to regulate water output onto a surface is the same control objective as the operator's spray-bar and fill-valve work, on an institution-controlled haul road.

roles.title: Drywall and Ceiling Tile Installers
roles.description: Apply plasterboard or other wallboard to ceilings or interior walls of buildings. Apply or mount acoustical tiles or blocks, strips, or sheets of shock-absorbing materials to ceilings and walls of buildings to reduce or reflect sound. Materials may be of decorative quality. Includes lathers who fasten wooden, metal, or rockboard lath to walls, ceilings, or partitions of buildings to provide support base for plaster, fireproofing, or acoustical material.

tasks.label: Read blueprints or other specifications to determine methods of installation, work procedures, or material or tool requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Measure and mark surfaces to lay out work, according to blueprints or drawings, using tape measures, straightedges or squares, and marking devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial new construction (office, healthcare, data center): lay out an entire floor of interior partitions on the bare concrete slab from the drawings/BIM — pull control dimensions, snap track lines, mark door and other rough openings, wall-type tags and dimensions — before metal-stud framing starts. Active jobsite: dust, debris, other trades working, changing conditions.

Tenant-improvement / renovation fit-out inside an existing building (hospital wing, office floor, school) after demolition: field-verify existing conditions, then measure and mark the new partition track lines, door openings and wall types on the existing floor per the drawings. Work area is a barricaded construction zone with as-found conditions.

Multifamily wood-frame or podium residential: repeat unit-by-unit partition layout on plywood subfloor decks per plans, mirrored and variant unit types, floor after floor; marks must carry through for framing, MEP and finishes.

Suspended acoustical ceiling grid layout per the reflected ceiling plan in a commercial space: establish ceiling height with a laser/water level, mark the perimeter wall-angle line around the room, calculate and mark centerlines and border-tile dimensions, and lay out main-runner and hanger-wire points overhead.

Layout marks on vertical and overhead building surfaces per drawings: soffit and bulkhead heights on existing walls and columns, furring/lath spacing marks, top-track lines on the deck, control-joint and window/door head-height marks — done with tape measure, square, level, pencil and chalk line on the erected structure.

sources.title: Comparison of dusty robotics and traditional layout methods (Construction Robotics, Springer)
sources.claim: Peer-reviewed case study of Dusty Robotics' FieldPrinter, an autonomous layout robot, performing drywall and MEP layout marking on the slab across an 8-floor medical office building ..., outperforming the manual two-person drywall layout crew on accuracy, labor hours and rework.

sources.title: Skanska Case Study | Dusty Robotics
sources.claim: Skanska used the Dusty FieldPrinter to print drywall, mechanical, electrical and plumbing layout directly on the construction site floor of a 3-story, 70,000 sq ft medical facility, reporting 100% layout accuracy and 50% faster layout.

sources.title: HP SitePrint Case Studies | HP Official Site
sources.claim: HP SitePrint, an autonomous layout robot that prints CAD/BIM lines, points and text on jobsite floors, is used by commercial drywall/framing contractors (e.g. Valley Interior Systems) and on hospital projects for interior wall-track layout, with one operator replacing a multi-person layout crew.

sources.title: HP SitePrint prints 2D plans on construction site floors - AEC Magazine
sources.claim: Dusty Robotics' FieldPrinter prints layout on the range of deck surfaces found on residential and commercial jobsites, including plywood subfloor and wood formwork, not only finished concrete slabs.

sources.title: Multi-Family Residential Projects | Dusty Robotics
sources.claim: Drywall subcontractor Daley's Drywall runs the Dusty FieldPrinter on multifamily floors, printing unit layouts on the deck across mirrored and variant unit types, reporting $300K labor savings and an 80% compression of layout.

sources.title: WEINMANN Multifunction Bridge WALLTEQ M-300 | HOMAG
sources.claim: WEINMANN WALLTEQ multifunction bridges are CNC gantries over fixtured element tables in prefabricated panel plants that process plasterboard and mark layout drawings onto the panel directly from the digital data record.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: CNC marking of layout geometry on wall/ceiling panels in prefab plants. It is the same measure-and-mark-from-drawings function on the same gypsum/sheathing materials, at equal or better precision, but with the surface fixtured on a machine table rather than erected in a building.

sources.title: WEINMANN multifunction bridges | HOMAG
sources.claim: WEINMANN multifunction bridges perform element planking tasks fully automatically and are used to produce wall, ceiling, roof and gable elements, with marking and labeling among the standard processing types.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated production and marking of wall and ceiling elements. Establishes that the same fixtured-gantry cell handles ceiling elements, so ceiling layout geometry can be marked by machine when the work is brought to it.

sources.title: Hilti — Digital Products Award Winner 2021 Jaibot | Building Transformations
sources.claim: Hilti's Jaibot locates, marks and drills BIM-specified overhead holes (including for overhead grid systems) on active construction sites, but an operator remote-drives the platform from one drilling position to the next, and it marks points rather than laying out ceiling-height or grid lines on walls.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: BIM-driven marking and drilling of overhead anchor points for suspended grid systems — the closest robotic analogue to ceiling layout marking, cited to show the limits of current in-situ ceiling layout automation.

tasks.label: Cut and screw together metal channels to make floor or ceiling frames, according to plans for the location of rooms or hallways.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New commercial construction (office/school/hospital shell): worker reads plans, snaps layout for rooms and hallways on the slab, cuts floor and ceiling track to length with snips/chop saw, shoots/screws track to the slab and to the deck above, then cuts and screws studs into the runners. Open floor plate shared with other trades, debris, out-of-level slabs, obstructions.

Suspended drywall/acoustical ceiling framing in a building under construction: cutting main carrying channels and hat/furring channels to length, tying/clipping and screwing them into a level grid off hanger wires or rod hangers, laser-leveled, cut and fitted around ducts, sprinklers and light fixtures.

Soffits, bulkheads, chases, drops and curved/radius framing: channel cut and screwed into one-off frames field-fitted around ductwork, beams and existing irregular conditions, dimensions taken in the field rather than from a clean plan.

Tenant improvement / renovation inside an existing occupied building (office suite, clinic, retail): framing new partitions per plans at night or in phased areas, scribing track to out-of-level floors and existing walls, working around furniture, live services and protection of finishes.

Off-site prefabrication in a contractor's panel shop: cutting cold-formed steel studs and track per shop drawings and screwing them into wall, floor and ceiling frames on squaring/framing tables, then bundling panels for delivery.

sources.system: Kawasaki BX200L / MX420L robot line at Sekisui Heim Kyushu plant
sources.title: Robots Build Housing Units | Industrial Robots by Kawasaki Robotics
sources.claim: At Sekisui Heim's housing factory, Kawasaki industrial robots pick previously welded steel posts and beams, set them into frame configuration on the fixture, and spot-weld the corners; additional robots assemble the ceiling, floor and gable ... of each housing unit on the production line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: factory assembly of steel floor and ceiling frames for housing units. It is the same operation the drywall/lathing task describes — positioning cut steel channel/beam members per a plan and joining them into a floor or ceiling frame — at comparable or tighter precision, differing only in that joints are spot-welded rather than screwed.

sources.system: Sekisui Heim robotic house-building line (Kyushu plant)
sources.title: Robotic House Construction—Sekisui Heim's Pursuit in Combating a Housing Industry Labor Shortage
sources.claim: The same Sekisui Heim line runs more than 30 different welding programs for different unit strength requirements, with robots replacing the three manual welders previously required, indicating programmed autonomous operation rather than teleoperation.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above (factory assembly of steel unit floor/ceiling frames); cited here to establish autonomy and production maturity of the frame-assembly cell.

sources.system: Robotic arm framing/fastening cells in CFS panel and pod fabrication shops
sources.developer: CFS prefabrication industry (reported by STRUCTURE Magazine / NCSEA)

sources.claim: In cold-formed steel panel shops, robotic arms weld stud-to-track joints and whole panels using weld positions defined in BIM/CAD with laser profile scanners checking frame deviation, and are also used for screwing studs to tracks with software-specified screw locations and spacing.
sources.transferJustification: Direct: joining light-gauge steel studs to track with screws per a digital plan is the fastening half of this task, performed on the same materials (CFS stud and track) inside fixtured shop cells.

sources.system: BIM-driven automated CFS roll-forming lines (e.g., FRAMECAD, Howick class machines) in panel plants
sources.developer: Steel Framing Industry Association (BuildSteel) reporting on CFS industry
sources.title: 5 Ways Robotic Automation Is Enhancing Cold-Formed Steel Construction — BuildSteel.org
sources.claim: Automated roll-forming machines driven by digital BIM models produce cold-formed steel studs and tracks cut precisely ... in the factory, replacing manual cutting of studs on site; the trade association cites OFFSITEK's Charlotte plant as a facility merging automation and robotic assembly.
sources.transferJustification: Covers the cutting half of the task: machine-controlled cutting/punching of channel members to plan dimensions, the factory substitute for cutting track and studs on site.

sources.title: OFFSITEK Combines Steel Framing with Offsite Technology to Manufacture Affordable Housing — BuildSteel.org
sources.claim: OFFSITEK, a Charlotte, North Carolina manufacturer, operates a factory that combines automation, robotic assembly and software to produce pre-engineered light-gauge steel framing panel systems for residential and commercial buildings.
sources.transferJustification: Named US plant producing light-gauge steel wall/floor framing panels with robotic assembly; corroborates that the E1 fabrication route is in commercial use, though the source does not detail autonomy.

sources.title: Dusty Robotics introduces FieldPrint Platform Gen 2 for enhanced construction efficiency
sources.claim: On real construction sites the deployed layout robot prints BIM wall layouts (including wall types and door openings) directly on the deck; more than 130 units were in the field, but the robot only marks lines — the channel cutting and fastening remains manual.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated jobsite layout of wall locations from BIM. It substantiates only the layout step of this task, not cutting or screwing channels, so it cannot support a positive E3 or E2 judgment for the framing work itself.

sources.title: Hilti unveils BIM-enabled construction robot for mobile ceiling work — Construction Dive
sources.claim: The most capable jobsite robot for overhead interior work is a semi-autonomous, BIM-driven ceiling-drilling robot: an operator drives it into position and it then drills anchor holes for MEP hangers; it does not cut or assemble framing members.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: BIM-driven overhead hole drilling on active jobsites. Cited to characterize the state of the art for in-situ ceiling work; it performs no channel cutting or frame assembly, so it supports no positive judgment for this task.

tasks.label: Hang drywall panels on metal frameworks of walls and ceilings in offices, schools, or other large buildings, using lifts or hoists to adjust panel heights, when necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Open office floor or school classroom wing under fit-out: hanging full-size 4x8 to 4x12 gypsum panels vertically on light-gauge metal stud partitions, floor to ceiling, in clear runs with no obstructions; lift the sheet, butt it tight, screw off the field and edges with a screw gun to the studs and track.

Same commercial partitions, but boards that must be measured, scribed, cut and fitted: around door and borrowed-light frames, at ends of runs and inside/outside corners, and cut-outs for electrical boxes, switch/data rings, sprinkler drops and duct penetrations, with tolerances tight enough that the finisher can tape the joints.

Large flat gypsum board ceiling in a corridor, lobby, restroom block or classroom: full-size panels lifted overhead onto metal furring channel / hat channel grid using a drywall panel lift or jack, screwed to the metal framing, working around already-installed hangers and ductwork above.

Elevated work from scissor lifts, scaffold or baker's staging: atrium, gymnasium, stairwell or high-corridor walls and tall shaft/partition board above the ceiling line, panels hoisted to height and fastened to metal framing at 15-30 ft.

Complex assemblies: multi-layer fire-rated and sound-rated walls, shaftwall systems with C-H studs and liner panels, curved/radius walls, soffits and bulkheads, congested MEP zones, and occupied-building renovation where existing conditions are out of square.

sources.system: Shimizu ceiling board construction robot (Robo-Buddy lineage)
sources.title: Development of Autonomous Robots for Construction (ISARC 2024)
sources.claim: Shimizu's ceiling construction robot is an autonomous two-arm mobile robot that attaches ~14 kg plasterboard to ceiling foundations (steel or wooden) with tapping screws; it carries its own lifter and screw magazine.

sources.system: Shimizu ceiling board construction robot + assist robot
sources.title: Development of Autonomous Robots for Construction (ISARC 2024)
sources.claim: The ceiling board robot plus its material-supply assist robot were applied at an actual construction site in Japan, installing 74 boards (123 m2), at roughly 8 minutes per board versus 6 minutes for a two-worker crew, replacing the output of two workers with one operator.

sources.title: A Production System for a New Era – The Shimizu Smart Site autonomous robots can transform a job site!
sources.claim: Robo-Buddy locates itself against BIM and the actual ceiling frame with laser sensors, drives itself to the work location, holds ceiling boards to the metal ceiling frame and screws them in.

sources.system: WEINMANN steel frame construction line (insert tables + multifunction bridge)
sources.title: Steel Frame Constructions | HOMAG
sources.claim: WEINMANN's off-site production portfolio includes automated attachment of sheathing materials to steel frame works, i.e. board fastened by CNC machinery onto light-gauge steel frames held on fixtured tables.

sources.system: WEINMANN WALLTEQ M-300 / M-500 multifunction bridge
sources.title: WEINMANN WALLTEQ Multi-Function Bridges - Stiles Machinery
sources.claim: The WALLTEQ multifunction bridge fastens sheathing to fixtured frames (M-500 screws as well as nails/staples) and routs rough openings and power outlet cut-outs in the fastened board automatically under CNC/DfMA control.

sources.title: FEEDBOT Series – Robotic Solutions | Stiles Machinery
sources.claim: The FEEDBOT W-500 robot picks and places sheathing panels onto the framed element with a vacuum suction head, integrating with the WALLTEQ fastening bridge, so placement as well as fastening is machine-performed.

sources.title: WEINMANN Multifunction Bridge WALLTEQ M-300 | HOMAG
sources.claim: The WALLTEQ bridge line is explicitly configured for plasterboard (gypsum board) processing, not only wood sheathing.

sources.claim: AIST's HRP-5P humanoid autonomously picked up a gypsum board and screwed it to a wall stud frame in a mock-up wall built in the lab; the demonstration was slow and confined to a prepared setting.

sources.system: Autonomous construction robot with telescopic arm for drywall panel installation
sources.title: Autonomous Construction Robot with Telescopic Arm for Drywall Panel Installation (ISARC 2025)
sources.claim: A 2025 research drywall panel installation robot with telescopic arm identifies runner locations by vision but is operated semi-automatically with remote monitoring and control, so it does not establish autonomous on-site wall panel hanging.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (drywall panel installation on runners/studs); cited to show the on-site wall-hanging state of the art remains operator-controlled rather than autonomous.

sources.title: Behind the Gloss: Construction's Dirty Work Is Going Robotic – Architect Magazine
sources.claim: Canvas robots perform drywall finishing (mudding and sanding) alongside crews inside active commercial construction interiors, but are described as semi-autonomous and do not hang board.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (drywall finishing on the same commercial interiors) cited only as context on robots working in E3 construction interiors; it does not lift or fasten panels, so it cannot substantiate hanging.

tasks.label: Fit and fasten wallboard or drywall into position on wood or metal frameworks, using glue, nails, or screws.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Commercial/institutional interior build-out: hanging 4x12 gypsum board (often 5/8" fire-rated, one or two layers) on light-gauge metal stud walls in an office, school, hospital or hotel under construction; boards carried in, aligned to layout, screwed off with a screwgun, working around door frames, in-wall MEP and shaft walls.

Commercial drywall ceilings ("hard lids") and soffits: lifting board overhead onto suspended metal furring/hat channel in open floor plates of a new building, screwing off from a baker's scaffold or lift, with penetrations for lights, sprinklers and diffusers handled by cut pieces.

Residential new construction walls: hanging 4x12 1/2" board horizontally on wood studs of a single-family house or townhome under construction; glue-and-screw or nail, tight to adjacent sheets, on an unfinished, cluttered floor.

Residential new-construction ceilings (lids): lifting full sheets overhead onto wood joists/trusses in a house, holding with a panel lift or partner, fastening with screws, working in small rooms with HVAC, wiring and can lights present.

Remodel, repair and patch work: fitting and fastening a board or partial board into an existing wall or ceiling in an occupied home, apartment or store, matching plane and thickness of surrounding surfaces around existing framing and utilities.

Off-site panelization/modular plant: fastening gypsum board onto framed wall panels or ceiling cassettes moving through a fixed production line, with boards fed from a stack and frames held on a work table.

sources.system: Shimizu ceiling construction robot (Robo-Buddy Ceiling) with ceiling assist robot
sources.title: Development of Autonomous Robots for Construction (ISARC 2024)
sources.claim: Shimizu's autonomous ceiling construction robot (two industrial arms on a mobile base, plus a material-supply assist robot) picks up ~14 kg plasterboard, presses it tight to already-installed boards and screws it to metal ceiling foundations; it was applied at a real construction site in Japan, installing 74 boards (123 m2) at about 8 minutes per board versus ~6 minutes for a pair of workers.

sources.title: A Production System for a New Era – Shimizu Smart Site autonomous robots
sources.claim: Shimizu describes the Robo-Buddy robots working on job sites: sensors locate the ceiling framing, one arm holds the ceiling board in position and the other drives screws, with the robot moving itself between work positions on the floor plate.

sources.title: 清水建設が天井施工ロボットをついに実用化、30年越しで開発成功 | 日経Robotics
sources.claim: Japanese trade press reports Shimizu put its ceiling installation robot into practical use, with one arm gripping the ceiling board and the other driving screws into the ceiling substrate; it was applied at a domestic construction site in March 2023 and completed the task successfully.

sources.system: Automated wall paneling robot cells at FingerHaus
sources.title: Automated wall production for prefabricated houses – Reference Projects
sources.claim: Beth Sondermaschinen built two robot cells at prefab housebuilder FingerHaus in which a robot, guided by a camera system that locates timber frames and plasterboard sheets, picks sheets with a vacuum gripper, positions them on the wall frame, changes to a stapler tool and fastens them; workers only inspect and approve.

sources.title: Randek – House Production Technologies – ZeroLabor
sources.claim: Randek's ZeroLabor robotic sheathing cell (two to five robots) automatically sheathes prefabricated wall panels, floor cassettes ... with multiple layers of OSB, plasterboard and other boards, selecting the next sheet, placing, fastening and routing it after an automated squaring table aligns the frame.

sources.system: Kawasaki BX250L robotic wall sheathing line (Rehkemper / SCADAware integration)
sources.title: Assembling Walls for Prefabricated Homes | Industrial Robots by Kawasaki
sources.claim: At a US prefab wall panel plant, four Kawasaki BX250L robots on gantry rails pick large sheathing panels, place them on framed wall panels, fasten them and rout out openings, running production for the housebuilder.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic sheathing of stud-framed wall panels with OSB rather than gypsum. Same sheet sizes, same pick-place-align-fasten operation on the same stud frames in the same factory cell, so it corroborates that board-on-frame fastening is a solved E1 operation.

sources.title: This humanoid robot can (slowly) install drywall all by itself
sources.claim: AIST's HRP-5P humanoid autonomously picked up an ~11 kg gypsum board, held it against a wall stud frame and screwed it in place, but the demonstration was slow and confined to a laboratory mock-up rather than a working site.

sources.system: Autonomous construction robot with telescopic arm for drywall panel installation
sources.title: Autonomous Construction Robot with Telescopic Arm for Drywall Panel Installation – IAARC
sources.claim: A 2025 ISARC paper presents a mobile drywall-panel installation robot with a telescopic arm, drills and nail guns, but it is operated semi-automatically through a web interface with remote monitoring and control by an operator.

tasks.label: Measure and cut openings in panels or tiles for electrical outlets, windows, vents, plumbing, or other fixtures, using keyhole saws or other cutting tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Residential new construction or remodel: hanging 1/2" gypsum board on wood-stud walls in a house under construction. Worker locates electrical outlet/switch boxes, transfers measurements to the sheet (or tacks the sheet over the box), and cuts the rectangular openings with a jab/keyhole saw or spiral cut-out tool so the box rings flush. Debris, other trades, and varying stud/box layouts on site.

Commercial interior build-out (offices, schools, healthcare) on metal studs and gypsum ceilings: measuring and cutting openings for HVAC diffusers, sprinkler drops, recessed lights, speakers, access panels and device boxes; much of it overhead from stilts or a lift, coordinated to MEP layout drawings.

Suspended acoustical ceiling tile work: measuring and cutting 2x2/2x4 mineral-fiber lay-in tiles on a bench or sawhorse to fit border cells and to accept sprinkler heads, downlights, diffusers and speakers; utility knife/straightedge and hole cutters, with fit tolerances hidden by escutcheons and trim rings.

Bathrooms, kitchens and other wet/service areas: cutting round and rectangular openings in moisture-resistant board or cement board for tub/shower valves, supply and drain stub-outs, exhaust fans, and recessed cabinets; tight quarters and close tolerances around escutcheons.

Large penetrations and openings: cutting board around window and door returns, soffits, beams and chases, and cutting rough openings in exterior gypsum sheathing; long straight cuts on full 4x8 to 4x12 sheets, often handled by two workers.

Cutting an opening into board that is already installed and finished, in an occupied or completed building: a new can-light or diffuser hole, an access panel in an existing ceiling, or a repair cut-out; the work must be done in place, overhead, with dust control and no way to remove the panel to a bench.

sources.title: WEINMANN Multifunction Bridge WALLTEQ M-300
sources.claim: The WEINMANN (HOMAG) WALLTEQ M-300 CNC multifunction bridge processes plasterboard/sheathing on wall, roof and ceiling elements and routs cut-outs such as electrical socket holes, working from the CAD/CAM data record over a clamped element table.

sources.title: The WALLTEQ M-300 multifunction bridge by WEINMANN – Wood Industry
sources.claim: Trade press describes the CNC-controlled WALLTEQ M-300 as producing door and window openings and socket recesses in the planking of prefabricated building elements.

sources.developer: HOMAG / WEINMANN, distributed by Stiles Machinery
sources.title: WEINMANN WALLTEQ Multi-Function Bridges - Stiles Machinery
sources.claim: The US distributor of WEINMANN multifunction bridges markets them for sheathing lines that automatically rout and drill rough openings, including window and door openings and power outlet cut-outs, in panel plants.

sources.system: WEINMANN multifunction bridges at Wolf Systembau plant
sources.title: Bridges build houses | HOMAG
sources.claim: In a working prefabricated-housing plant (Wolf Systembau), the installed WEINMANN multifunction bridges cut all recesses in the fastened planking, including the window openings.

sources.system: flextos SUPERCUT CNC (and Hybrid CNC) gypsum board router/saw table
