tasks.label: Test components or circuits of faulty equipment to locate defects, using oscilloscopes, signal generators, ammeters, voltmeters, or special diagnostic software programs.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In-store or IT-bench triage of a customer's computer or mobile device (laptop, desktop, tablet, phone, peripheral) brought in for repair: the tech powers it up, runs vendor/third-party diagnostic software and functional tests, checks adapter/PSU output with a meter, and isolates the failed subsystem (drive, battery, display, board, power supply). Device sits on a bench in a retail repair back room or corporate IT room.

Depot/shop board-level fault localization on a PCB removed from a printer, PC, POS terminal or ATM module: tech probes test points with DMM, oscilloscope, signal generator or analog-signature comparison against a known-good board/schematic to identify the failed component before rework.

On-site service call on an office copier/MFP or production printer at a customer office, school or print shop: enter the machine's service diagnostic mode, read fault codes, then open panels and measure voltages/continuity at connectors, sensor outputs and the low/high-voltage power supply with a meter to isolate a failed board, sensor or harness while the machine is in place.

ATM service call at a bank branch or retail/convenience site: run the vendor diagnostic utility, exercise and test the dispenser, card reader, encryptor and receipt modules in place, measure supply rails and sensor signals with a meter to isolate the faulty module, working in a customer-facing lobby or through-the-wall installation.

On-site diagnosis of networked PCs, POS terminals, self-service kiosks and desktop printers at customer premises taken as found (retail sales floors, warehouses, small businesses, home offices): trace cabling with meters/testers, run diagnostic utilities on the unit, measure power at outlets and connectors, and isolate the defective component amid live operations and cluttered, site-specific layouts.

sources.title: Electronic Board Testing: ICT, Flying Probe & Functional | SPEA
sources.claim: SPEA sells flying-probe test systems configured for repair centers that automatically probe a fixtured board and identify the faulty component, producing a component-level diagnostic report — i.e., locating defects in faulty electronic assemblies.

sources.system: Huntron Access / Access 2 Prober with Huntron Workstation and Tracker
sources.title: Flying Probe Technology that Replaces Conventional Test Fixtures | Huntron
sources.claim: Huntron Access flying-probe stations automate probing of circuit-board test points that would otherwise be done by hand, driving a Tracker (analog signature analysis), DMM, spectrum analyzer or other instrument under software control to troubleshoot and isolate component faults on a board fixtured in the prober.

sources.system: MATT device test automation robot (with M360 diagnostics)
sources.title: M360 and ADAPTA Robotics integrate diagnostics into MATT testing robot – Mobile News
sources.claim: Adapta Robotics' MATT device-testing robot, which physically manipulates devices held in cradles inside its cell and runs third-party diagnostic suites on them, has over 100 units deployed at recommerce and consumer-electronics operations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated functional/diagnostic testing of refurbished devices. It is the same act as bench triage — running diagnostic software and functional tests on a suspect computer/mobile device to identify which component has failed — on the same class of objects.

sources.title: Refurbished Device Diagnostics | MATT Robot Testing Automation
sources.claim: MATT automates diagnostic testing of refurbished electronics including laptops and tablets by physically interacting with the ... (touch, buttons, screens) inside its test cabinet while diagnostics software records the failing functions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: end-of-line/refurbishment functional diagnostics. Same devices and same diagnostic software the repairer uses; the robot supplies the physical interaction needed to run the tests to a defect verdict.

sources.title: In-Circuit Test Systems | Keysight
sources.claim: In-circuit test systems are commercial automated diagnostic machines that verify and diagnose individual components on a fixtured printed circuit board, corroborating that component-level defect location is a solved purpose-built-machine capability.

sources.system: Microsoft Research modular data center robotics
sources.title: Microsoft Research details early-stage modular robotics for data centers - DCD
sources.claim: Robotic hardware servicing inside structured facilities (data centers) remains early-stage research at partial autonomy, indicating no fielded robot performs in-situ diagnosis of installed equipment in human work facilities.
sources.transferJustification: Closest analogue to in-situ electronic equipment servicing inside a controlled facility; it shows the capability is not yet demonstrated autonomously, supporting the negative E2 judgments.

tasks.label: Clean, oil, or adjust mechanical parts to maintain machines' operating efficiency and to prevent breakdowns.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scheduled preventive maintenance visit on an office copier/MFP at a customer's business office: open covers and access panels, vacuum toner and paper dust, wipe feed/registration/transfer rollers and separation pads with solvent cloths, clean optics and sensors, grease fuser and drive gears, adjust registration/belt tension, reassemble and run test prints.

PM on an ATM or self-service kiosk at a bank branch or retail site: clean card-reader head and receipt/journal printer path, clean and lubricate note-transport belts, rollers and dispenser/presenter module, clear paper and note dust, clean sensors, adjust transport and reassemble under time and security constraints while the machine is out of service.

PM on high-volume production printers, folders/inserters or mail-finishing equipment in a print shop or in-plant mail center: wipe paper dust from the paper path and vacuum debris, oil chains, cams and bearings, check and adjust timing/registration and belt tension, replace worn feed tires.

Bench work in a repair shop or depot: a desktop, laptop, server or a removed machine subassembly (feed-roller assembly, fuser, shredder cutter head) is on the bench; technician opens the case, blows/vacuums out dust, cleans fans and heatsinks, reapplies thermal compound or grease to rails and gears, and reassembles and tests.

Maintenance of machines in uncontrolled settings: a printer in a cluttered home office, a POS/receipt printer behind a busy retail counter, a copier in a crowded storeroom — cramped access, no fixed layout, machine must be pulled out, cleaned and lubricated in place around customers and furniture.

sources.system: DTI laptop refurbishing robot (Laptop Disassembling Robot, RoboSAPIENS)
sources.title: Search-based Robustness Testing of Laptop Refurbishing Robotic Software
sources.claim: Danish Technological Institute laptop refurbishing robots use vision-based screw/sticker detection to automate disassembly, cleaning and reassembly of used laptops at a robotic workstation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: laptop refurbishment. It covers the same physical acts as bench-level cleaning PM on computers — vision-located screw removal to open a case, cleaning of surfaces, and reassembly — on the same class of objects (used laptops/PCs) at comparable precision, in a purpose-built robot workstation.

sources.system: Automated 3D-printer maintenance cell (KUKA LBR iiwa 7-DOF arm + ROBOTIQ gripper, Ender 3 V2 printer)
sources.developer: Monash University (Andrews, Granland, Chen, Tang, Chen)
sources.title: Automated 3D-Printer Maintenance and Part Removal by Robotic Arms
sources.claim: A KUKA arm with a Robotiq gripper autonomously operates and maintains a fused-filament printer: removing parts, cleaning the printer bed, applying adhesive, and monitoring bed levelness so the machine can keep running.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: routine maintenance of a printing machine. It is the same task type — cleaning a machine's working surface, applying a consumable substance, and checking an adjustment (bed level) to keep the machine operating — but only on one fixed, known printer whose position is engineered for the arm.

sources.system: DOPAG production cell for automated grease metering
sources.title: Production cell for automated grease metering | DOPAG
sources.claim: A commercial six-axis robot cell meters grease onto plastic gearwheels presented on workpiece carriers, applying lubricant to interior and exterior surfaces with spray and shot valves.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: lubricant application in manufacturing. It substantiates the 'oil mechanical parts' element on gear-type components of the same scale, but only where the part is fixtured on a carrier in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: EVST collaborative robot automated cleaning & air-blow cell
sources.title: Collaborative Robot Automated Cleaning & Air-Blow Cell — Engine Parts
sources.claim: A commercial collaborative-robot cell performs automated cleaning of machined parts, driving an air knife along a programmed path to blow debris out of surfaces, blind holes and cavities.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic blow-off cleaning of parts. It is the same physical act as blowing dust out of a computer chassis, fans and heatsinks, at comparable precision, but requires the workpiece at preset positions in a cell.

sources.system: Tianxun (2nd generation) data center maintenance robot
sources.title: The slow rise of robots in the data center - DCD
sources.claim: Alibaba reports a second-generation Tianxun robot operating in five of its data centers that autonomously inspects, locates and replaces faulty hard disks; Google is only testing similar drive-handling robots and its data center VP notes such tasks are more complicated than in other robotized industries.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: in-facility maintenance of computer hardware. It marks the frontier of what robots do inside a structured human facility — swapping a hot-plug module in a purpose-designed rack — and involves no cleaning, lubrication or mechanical adjustment, so it does not carry over to this task.

tasks.label: Align, adjust, or calibrate equipment according to specifications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Multifunction copier/printer at a customer's office: after a repair or during preventive maintenance, the tech runs the service mode, performs image registration and color/density calibration from test prints, and makes mechanical adjustments (paper-feed skew guides, doc-feeder alignment, transfer/fuser gaps, finisher/stapler position), iterating until output meets the manufacturer's spec sheet.

ATM at a bank branch or retail lobby: adjust and calibrate card reader, note-thickness/double-detect sensors, dispenser and depositor transport alignment, receipt printer registration and touchscreen calibration, then verify with test cards, test notes and test transactions against the OEM service specification, working in a live public-facing space with the unit partly out of service.

Production print / high-volume equipment in a print shop or in-plant reprographics center: densitometer/spectrophotometer and color-profile calibration, print-head or drum registration, sheet-feed and finishing (folder, booklet-maker, cutter) adjustments on a large fixed machine, judged against customer color and registration tolerances.

Desktop/laptop/workstation and peripherals after board, display or drive service: monitor color/brightness calibration with a colorimeter, touchscreen and digitizer calibration, sensor/hinge/connector alignment, bar-code scanner and printer alignment, done on a depot bench or at the user's desk in a corporate office.

Other office/business machines at a customer facility: mail inserters and folders, check/document scanners, postage meters, shredders, POS terminals and self-service kiosks — setting feed-guide positions, belt tensions, sensor thresholds and stop positions per the service manual, then running test batches until jam and skew rates meet spec.

Service call at a home office or very small unattended business site: printer/MFP or PC and peripherals sitting in a cluttered, non-standard space with no institutional control; tech aligns paper guides, runs head-alignment/calibration routines and adjusts the device in place before verifying output.

sources.system: Fori Automation robotic toe-set / wheel alignment system
sources.title: End of Line Testing Systems - Wheel Aligners, Headlamp Aimers, Robotic Toe Set & Automated Tooling Changeover - Fori Automation
sources.claim: Fori Automation builds robotic end-of-line wheel-alignment stations in which robots measure a parameter and drive mechanical adjusters (tie-rod hex, cam bolt) to bring it inside a tight specification, then torque the lock nut — a closed-loop measure/adjust/verify cycle on a fixtured product.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: vehicle wheel alignment at end of line. It is the same action class as this task — measure against a spec, turn a mechanical adjuster with a driven socket, re-measure, lock the adjustment to torque — performed autonomously on a workpiece presented in a fixtured, purpose-built station, at tighter tolerance than office-machine registration adjustments.

sources.title: Kasalis Introduces Pixid 700 Platform for Emerging Technologies in LiDAR, AR/VR Applications and Vehicle Display Projection Systems
sources.claim: Kasalis Pixid systems perform fully automated active optical alignment and calibration of camera and optical modules to sub-micron/nanometre positioning specifications in production machines, used on millions of devices.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: active alignment of optical modules during manufacture. It is alignment to specification using live sensor feedback on a fixtured device — the same loop used when aligning a scanner optic, laser/polygon assembly or print head in an office machine, at far tighter precision.

sources.system: ASG AX-10 robotic assembly cell with X-PAQ screwdriving system
sources.developer: ASG, a Division of Jergens Inc.
sources.title: Robotic Cell Automates Screwdriving Process | ASSEMBLY
sources.claim: Commercially available benchtop robotic assembly cells fixture a product and drive small fasteners (#000 to #10) with torque- and angle-controlled electric screwdrivers to tight tolerances.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated fastening in a fixtured cell. Office-machine adjustment work is largely loosening, repositioning and re-torquing small screws, eccentrics and guide brackets of exactly this size class; the cell supplies the fixturing, positional repeatability and torque control such adjustments require.

sources.system: ABB YuMi ATM test robot (Abrantix / Diebold Nixdorf ATMs)
sources.title: ABB's YuMi robot automates ATM testing for more reliable banking
sources.claim: A dual-arm ABB YuMi robot in an Abrantix test lab operates Diebold Nixdorf ATMs unattended overnight — inserting cards, entering PINs, and withdrawing and depositing notes — to verify ATM behaviour against specifications.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: ATM functional test. It covers the verification half of ATM adjustment/calibration work — driving the customer interface, feeding cards and notes and checking the machine against spec — on an ATM presented in a fixed position to the robot, the same objects and precision as the technician's verification passes.

sources.system: OptoFidelity TOUCH automated touch/HMI test system
sources.title: TOUCH: Automated touch screen testing | OptoFidelity
sources.claim: OptoFidelity's TOUCH is a commercially delivered robotic platform with instrumented fingertips that autonomously operates and measures touch user interfaces on production and lab devices, with motion accuracy verified to about ±25 µm.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic touchscreen test. Alignment/calibration of copiers, ATMs and kiosks is driven from a touch service menu and verified by measurement; this system shows a robot can autonomously navigate a device's touch UI and measure the result to spec in a fixtured cell.

sources.system: Xerox Automated Color Quality Suite (ACQS) inline spectrophotometer
sources.title: Xerox Color J75 Press brochure
sources.claim: Xerox digital presses ship with an inline spectrophotometer that performs press colour/density calibration automatically on a schedule, closing the print–measure–adjust loop without an operator or technician.
sources.transferJustification: Same task, machine-embedded: the colour/density calibration a technician would perform with charts and a handheld spectrophotometer is executed by the machine's own sensing and actuation; it does not cover the mechanical registration and feed adjustments in the same service instance.

sources.title: Apple expands global recycling programs - Apple
sources.claim: Apple's Daisy line autonomously disassembles 23 iPhone models at 200 units per hour, removing covers, fasteners and modules from small consumer electronics on a purpose-built robotic line.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic teardown of small electronics. Reaching an adjustment point in an office machine or PC first requires removing covers, screws and modules; Daisy shows this access work done autonomously at production rate on fixtured devices of several models.

tasks.label: Fill machines with toners, inks, or other duplicating fluids.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Service call at a business customer's office: technician walks to a floor-standing MFP/copier, opens the front cover, releases and withdraws the spent toner cartridge, swaps the waste-toner bottle, seats and latches the new cartridge, vacuums/wipes spilled toner, closes covers, runs test prints and resets the counter. Machine models and office layouts vary site to site.

Production print center, in-plant reprographics, or school district duplicating room: refill a high-volume press's toner hopper from bulk bottles, or swap ink cartridges/ink packs in digital duplicators (Riso-type) and production copiers, prime the supply, clear toner spill, and run quality test sheets.

Bench/depot work in the repairer's own service shop: after a rebuild or refurbishment, charge the machine with toner/developer or ink, prime the supply lines, run test prints and verify density before shipping the unit back to the customer.

Wide-format plotter or inkjet system at an engineering firm, sign shop, or hospital imaging department: install ink cartridges into slots or refill bulk ink tanks from bottles without dripping, purge/prime the printheads, and verify print output.

Small residential/home-office call: printer or small copier sitting on a desk in a cluttered home, uncertain access and lighting; technician fills or replaces ink/toner, cleans up any spill, and checks print quality.

sources.system: Ricoh automated toner filling machine / robot-based toner cartridge assembly line
sources.title: Automating the Toner Cartridge Production Line | Global | Ricoh
sources.claim: Ricoh runs automated toner-filling machines and robot-based assembly systems on its toner cartridge production lines, filling toner powder into bottles/cartridges in purpose-built lines at plants, logistics bases and sales companies.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: metered filling of toner powder into a machine-side container and robotic assembly of the cartridge. Under the E1 counterfactual the copier's toner reservoir or cartridge is presented fixtured to the filling nozzle, which is exactly the operation these lines perform, with the same material (toner powder) and dose accuracy.

sources.title: BMW Group deploys Figure 03 humanoid after tests with previous version - The Robot Report
sources.claim: Figure 02 humanoid worked 11 months in BMW's Spartanburg body shop inserting sheet-metal parts ..., a task requiring speed and placement accuracy, supporting production of 30,000+ vehicles.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: repeated precise insertion of a rigid part into a fixtured station in an industrial cell. Installing a toner or ink cartridge presented in a known pose at an E1 station requires comparable object handling and insertion precision, so performance carries over at E1 only.

sources.title: Mini dose | High Precision | Automatic | Filling Machine | Accutek
sources.claim: Accutek's Accu-Doser is an automatic multi-head precision dispensing machine that fills small bottles, vials and cartridges with 0.1-200 mL of liquid.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: precise metered filling of small containers with liquid. At E1 the printer's ink tank or cartridge arrives fixtured under the nozzle, so filling it with ink is the same operation at the same volumes and drip-free precision.

sources.system: Tianxun (2nd generation) data center maintenance robot
sources.date: 2026-06 (article), deployment reported in five data centers
sources.title: The slow rise of robots in the data center - DCD
sources.claim: Alibaba says its second-generation Tianxun robot operates in five of its data centers, autonomously locating and replacing faulty hard disks in about four minutes per disk.
sources.transferJustification: Closest E2 analogue: swapping a modular consumable component in IT equipment inside an institution-controlled facility. It transfers only partially - the drives sit in standardized rack slots at surveyed coordinates with no hinged covers, latches, loose powder or per-model variation - so it does not substantiate a copier toner change in an office.

tasks.label: Lay cable and hook up electrical connections between machines, power sources, and phone lines.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Deskside/office hookup: technician sets up or relocates a PC, multifunction copier/fax or POS terminal in an occupied office suite — plugs the power cord into a strip/UPS, runs a patch cord from the wall jack to the machine, connects an RJ11 fax line, dresses cables through desk grommets and under furniture, and verifies link and dial tone.

Structured cabling run in an occupied building: pull new Cat6/fiber runs from an IDF through drop ceilings, walls, raceway or floor conduit to workstation locations; support and dress the cable, terminate keystone jacks and patch-panel positions, label and test each run.

ATM or self-service kiosk install at a bank branch or retail site: bring dedicated AC power to the machine (cord/whip to a dedicated circuit or junction box), run and connect the network drop or legacy telephone line, route and secure cabling inside the pedestal/enclosure and through the floor sleeve, then power up and confirm host communication.

Server room / IDF / data-center work: rack a server or switch, run copper patch cords and fiber jumpers between the device, patch panels and switches, connect redundant PDU power cords, dress and label cabling in vertical/horizontal managers, verify links.

Residential home office or in-home small-business call: set up computer, printer and router; run cable along baseboards or through a wall plate, connect to the household phone jack and to available outlets, and tidy the cabling in a space taken as found.

sources.system: Universal Robots UR7e cobots + Cambrian AI vision (data-center cabling cell)
sources.developer: Teradyne Robotics / Universal Robots with Cambrian Robotics
sources.title: The AI Trainer, the Generalist and the Cable Inserter Walk into a Booth | Machine Design
sources.claim: Two UR7e collaborative robots guided by Cambrian's AI 3D vision system autonomously routed and inserted copper cabling to assemble high-density server racks, with the vision system reading connector orientation and adjusting trajectories in real time before insertion — i.e., laying cable and making connections in a fixtured robotic work cell.
sources.transferJustification: Same objects (copper data cables, latching connectors, rack equipment) and same acts (routing cable, inserting connectors) as the task's cabling and hook-up work, performed in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: Averex robotic wiring centre (and Rittal Wire Terminal); Polygon 'Wirebot'
sources.title: Automated Control Cabinet Wiring Solution for Scalable Renewable Energy Systems (SpringerLink chapter)
sources.claim: The Kiesling/Rittal Averex robotic wiring centre is a portal-robot machine that cuts and crimps wire, connects both ends to terminals and routes the wire inside the enclosure, automating what is otherwise manual point-to-point wiring between devices and power terminals.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = control-cabinet wiring: identical primitives to 'lay cable and hook up electrical connections between machines and power sources' (route conductor along a path, land both ends on terminals), at comparable precision, in a machine cell.

sources.system: Telescent G5 Network Topology Manager (robotic patch panel)
sources.title: Telescent Introduces Highest Density Optical Circuit Switches for 1.6T DR4 and DR8 Interconnects in GPU Clusters (Business Wire)
sources.claim: Telescent's G4/G5 Network Topology Manager is a commercially deployed robotic patch-panel/optical circuit switch that physically makes and breaks fiber cross-connects between network elements under software control inside its own rack enclosure at hyperscale and carrier data centers.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the data-center part of the task: physically connecting cable between machines (patching), but confined to a purpose-built robotic panel rather than the open data hall.

sources.system: HIL-SERL (human-in-the-loop sample-efficient RL) on Franka arms
sources.title: Precise and Dexterous Robotic Manipulation via Human-in-the-Loop Reinforcement Learning
sources.claim: HIL-SERL learned policies achieved 100% success on precise real-world manipulation including USB grasp-and-insertion and cable clipping/routing on a fixtured bench, running autonomously after training.
sources.transferJustification: Related tasks = USB connector insertion and cable clipping/routing: the same connector-mating precision and deformable-cable handling required to plug data/power cords into machines, shown at worker-level reliability in a fixtured cell.

sources.system: Komax Zeta 620 G2 / Omega harness assembly machines
sources.title: Harness Manufacturing | Komax
sources.claim: Komax harness and cabinet-wiring machines (e.g., Zeta 620 G2) automate cutting, crimping, labeling, housing/terminal insertion and routing of wires for control-cabinet construction — fully automatic wire-to-terminal connection in an industrial machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = automated harness/cabinet wiring; the wire preparation, connector-housing insertion and routing steps mirror making up and landing cables between equipment and power terminals, in a fixtured machine.

sources.system: Rocsys Steward / Rocsys autonomous charging robot
sources.title: Rocsys launches integrated platform to enable hands-free charging for autonomous mobility | Charged EVs
sources.claim: Rocsys' vision-guided robotic charging system autonomously detects a vehicle's arrival, opens the charge port, inserts the connector, charges and unplugs; it has been demonstrated with customer fleets at port terminals such as APM Terminals Maasvlakte II.
sources.transferJustification: Related task = making a power connection to a machine at a variable pose inside a human work facility; shows single-connector insertion only, at a dedicated bay, not cable running or multi-connector hook-up.

sources.title: Video shows robotic installation Cat 6 cabling above drop ceiling | Cabling Installation & Maintenance
sources.claim: The only publicised above-drop-ceiling communication-cable installation robot (Inspector Bots 'Minibot' pulling Cat 6) is driven by a remote human operator watching a camera feed, not autonomous.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the in-building cable-pulling instance; cited to show the demonstrated system is teleoperated and therefore cannot support a positive judgment.

tasks.label: Train new repairers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Field ride-along: an experienced ATM/office-machine technician brings a new hire on service calls at bank branches and customer offices, narrating the diagnostic reasoning, showing how a jam-prone cash dispenser or copier feed assembly is serviced, then watching the trainee attempt the job and correcting technique, tool use, and safety/security practice through verbal feedback.

Bench/classroom session at the service depot or training room: the trainer walks a group of new repairers through a machine's subsystems using a training unit, demonstrates teardown and reassembly steps, points out failure modes and part identification, and questions trainees to check understanding.

Desk-based instruction on procedures and systems: explaining service manuals and schematics, fault-code lookup, warranty and parts-ordering workflow, ticketing/dispatch software, customer-site etiquette, ESD, and cash-handling/security rules; reviewing the trainee's documentation and paperwork.

Remote coaching: a senior repairer talks a newer technician through an unfamiliar fault by phone, video call, or chat while the trainee is on site, prompting checks and interpreting readings until the trainee resolves the call.

Customer-site onboarding for a specific account: briefing a new repairer on that site's equipment fleet, escalation contacts, access and badging rules, and service-level expectations, then observing the first few calls and giving a performance debrief.

tasks.label: Calibrate testing instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Service-depot/shop bench: technician verifies and adjusts handheld electrical test instruments (digital multimeters, clamp meters, insulation/ground and ESD testers) against a bench multifunction calibrator or reference standard, records as-found/as-left readings, applies correction or calibration sticker.

Customer premises (bank branch, corporate office, print room, data closet): quick pre-use calibration of a portable test instrument — nulling DMM lead resistance, running an instrument self-cal, setting reference on a network/cable certifier with reference cords, zeroing a light/field meter — before diagnosing an ATM, PC or copier.

Shop bench: periodic calibration/verification of bench test gear — oscilloscope self-cal and probe compensation, function/signal generator, power supply, LCR meter — against traceable reference standards, with closed-case adjustment or entry of correction constants.

Calibration of non-electrical service and test tools used on office machines: torque screwdrivers/wrenches, belt-tension and thickness/feeler gauges, dial indicators, and print-quality densitometers/light meters, checked against reference gauges or standards on a bench.

Machine-specific test fixtures and jigs for ATMs and cash handlers: calibrating note-thickness/double-detect sensor gauges, currency-validator reference notes, card-reader test cards and dispenser test jigs, usually in the branch or at the depot with the target machine present.

sources.system: Trescal DMM robot and gage block robot (lab automation cells)
sources.title: Innovation | Trescal Worldwide
sources.claim: Trescal, the largest independent operator of calibration laboratories, states that DMM and gage-block robots in its labs automatically calibrate dozens of instruments within hours, running 24/7 while technicians handle harder work.
sources.transferJustification: Same task: calibration of testing instruments (handheld DMMs and gauges), the instrument class this occupation calibrates, performed in a purpose-built robotic cell inside a calibration lab.

sources.system: Trescal Calibration Robot (NI LabVIEW / NI Vision based)
sources.developer: Trescal (with CN Rood / National Instruments toolchain)
sources.title: CN Rood on LinkedIn: Trescal Calibration Robot
sources.claim: A Trescal calibration robot performs fully automatic calibration of digital ..., using NI LabVIEW and NI Vision to drive the sequence and read the meters' displays.

sources.system: KUKA LBR iiwa on flexFELLOW platform loading a Hexagon coordinate measuring machine
sources.developer: KUKA / Hexagon at Perschmann Calibration GmbH
sources.title: Automated calibration process at Perschmann Calibration GmbH with the sensitive KUKA robot - International Federation of Robotics
sources.claim: At Perschmann Calibration GmbH a KUKA LBR iiwa robot on a flexFELLOW platform has since December 2017 identified incoming measuring instruments, blown off dust, clamped them into the fixture of a coordinate measuring machine that runs the calibration, then unloaded them — in three-shift operation with ~0.5 µm precision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic handling and calibration of mechanical/dimensional measuring instruments (gauges, setting rings, pins). Transfers to calibrating a repairer's mechanical test tools — same object scale, tighter precision, same load/fixture/measure/unload cycle in a purpose-built cell.

sources.system: Fluke MET/CAL with 5500A/5520A calibrators and 8508A reference multimeter
sources.title: MET/CAL LITE Calibration Management Software (Fluke datasheet)
sources.claim: Fluke's MET/CAL calibration management software drives multifunction calibrators and reference multimeters to run automated computer-aided, closed-case and closed-loop calibration procedures on instruments under test, the standard automated bench used in accredited electrical cal labs.
sources.transferJustification: Same task, stimulus/measure/adjust portion: once the instrument is fixtured and connected (the E1 premise), the calibrator hardware physically sources traceable signals and closed-case adjustment is written to the instrument without human manipulation.

roles.title: Radio, Cellular, and Tower Equipment Installers and Repairers
aliases: RF Test Tech (Radio Frequency Test Technician)
Voice and Radio Technician (Voice and Radio Tech)
roles.description: Repair, install, or maintain mobile or stationary radio transmitting, broadcasting, and receiving equipment, and two-way radio communications systems used in cellular telecommunications, mobile broadband, ship-to-shore, aircraft-to-ground communications, and radio equipment in service and emergency vehicles. May test and analyze network coverage.

tasks.label: Inspect completed work to ensure all hardware is tight, antennas are level, hangers are properly fastened, proper support is in place, or adequate weather proofing has been installed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Macro cell site (monopole/lattice/guyed tower, 100-300 ft, fenced compound): hands-on post-construction/close-out inspection of a completed antenna swap or new build. Tech climbs, wrench- or torque-checks antenna, mount pipe and mount-to-tower hardware, tugs coax/hybrid hangers and stand-offs, confirms mount support, hand-checks connector weatherproofing (butyl/self-amalgamating tape, boots) and grounding kits; outdoor weather, harnessed at height.

Macro tower site: visual/photographic close-out audit and antenna alignment verification of a completed install - antennas plumb/level, azimuth and downtilt as-built vs. as-designed, hangers and mount steel present and fastened, weatherproofing and torque marks visibly in place, no missing hardware. Deliverable is a photo/measurement audit report; no wrench work.

Rooftop or building-mounted site (parapet/sled mounts, penthouse walls, cable tray runs): hands-on inspection of completed work - antenna level and mount bolts tight, sled ballast and support in place, hangers/tray clamps fastened, connector weatherproofing and roof penetration sealing checked by hand; congested rooftop, landlord-controlled premises.

Small cell / DAS node on a streetlight, utility or wood pole in the public right-of-way: from a bucket truck, verify shroud and antenna mounting hardware tight and level, banding/brackets secure, fiber and power connections sealed and weatherproofed, disconnect and meter enclosures gasketed and closed; traffic, pedestrians, varying pole types.

Ground level at the compound/shelter: inspect completed work at the base - coax/fiber entry ports and boots sealed, ice bridge and cable ladder hardware tight and supported, ground bar lugs torqued with anti-oxidant applied, cabinet doors gasketed and weather-tight, tower base plate bolts and grout condition.

Fleet shop / garage: inspect a completed mobile radio and antenna installation in a police car, ambulance, service truck or boat - roof/trunk antenna mount tight and sealed against water intrusion, NMO gasket seated, coax routed and secured with clamps/loom, control head and radio bracket bolts tight, power leads fused and strain-relieved.

sources.title: Scaling Cell Tower Inspections with 3D Tower Scan | Skydio

tasks.label: Run appropriate power, ground, or coaxial cables.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cell tower / monopole trunk run: hoist and run 1-5/8" coax or hybrid fiber-power trunk cable from the base equipment area up 100-250 ft to the antenna mounts, install hoisting grip, secure with cable hangers/clamps every ~3 ft on the tower leg or waveguide ladder, dress into the ice bridge and cabinet entry port. Outdoor, at height, wind/weather, each tower structure and route different.

Site grounding runs: run #6/#2 tinned copper ground conductors from the tower ground bar, coax grounding kits, ice bridge, cabinets and generator to the buried ground ring or ground rods; route down tower legs, bond with two-hole lugs or exothermic (Cadweld) connections, bury/backfill. Outdoor compound, soil, varied site layout.

Ground-level cabinet/shelter power cabling: run #6-#1/0 DC power and ground cables from the rectifier plant / breaker panel through ladder rack and cable tray to BBUs, radios and DC distribution in an equipment shelter or outdoor cabinet at a fenced, carrier-controlled cell site; strip, lug, torque, label and dress the runs.

Rooftop or in-building site (DAS, small cell, broadcast): pull coax/hybrid cable from a rooftop equipment room or telecom closet across the roof, through sleeves, conduit, cable trays and ceiling plenums to antenna locations; fire-stop and weatherproof penetrations. Layout differs building to building, congested with other trades' cable.

Mobile/vehicle radio install: in a fleet garage bay, run the fused power cable from the battery through a firewall grommet, route ground cable to a chassis stud, and run antenna coax from a roof- or trunk-mounted antenna under trim/carpet to the radio head in a police, fire or utility vehicle; secure with clips and loom.

tasks.label: Test operation of tower transmission components, using sweep testing tools or software.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Macro cell site commissioning/maintenance sweep: at a fenced tower compound, tech disconnects jumpers at the RRU/cabinet and (with a partner aloft or loads installed at top) connects a cable-and-antenna analyzer (e.g., Anritsu Site Master), performs OSL calibration, sweeps return loss/VSWR and distance-to-fault on each sector's feedline, torques connectors, and saves traces for the close-out package. Outdoors, variable weather, layout differs site to site.

Trouble ticket on a high-VSWR/return-loss alarm: tech sweeps the suspect line at several points (bottom of run, at jumpers, at the antenna port), swaps in loads, uses DTF to localize the reflection to a specific connector or damaged section, and re-sweeps after the fix to confirm the line meets spec. Live site, sector out of service, time pressure.

Rooftop, small-cell or in-building DAS sweep: cramped, non-standard rooftop or ceiling-space layouts, hatches and ladders, mixed vendor equipment; sweeping coax runs, jumpers and DAS antenna lines and documenting results.

Bench/staging sweep in a shop, warehouse or fleet garage: pre-testing jumpers, feedline reels, antennas, duplexers/filters, or sweeping the antenna line of a public-safety/vehicle two-way radio installation with an analyzer or service monitor; controlled indoor space, parts brought to the technician.

Indoor transmitter building or carrier equipment room (broadcast AM/FM/TV site, C-RAN hub): network-analyzer sweeps of rigid transmission line, combiners and the antenna system from the interior test port; fixed layout, standard racks, institution-controlled premises.

Ground-level work in the fenced site compound or equipment shelter: install surge arrestors/lightning protection at the cable entry port, land and terminate hardline transmission lines onto radios and cabinets, install grounding kits and jumpers on standard racks and ice bridges maintained by the carrier/tower owner.

Land mobile radio / mobile installs: mount NMO or mast antennas on service, emergency or marine vehicles and small buildings, drill and seal the mount, route and terminate coax to the radio, add surge arrestors on base-station feeds; done mostly in a fleet shop bay or a small radio room.

tasks.label: Replace existing antennas with new antennas as directed.

instances.label: Macro cell-site sector antenna swap on a lattice tower, monopole or self-support structure: crew climbs 80–300 ft, rigs a capstan hoist, disconnects and unwraps weatherproofed jumper connections, unbolts and lowers 40–90 lb panel antennas, hoists and clamps new antennas to the pipe mount, torques hardware, mates and weatherproofs RF/fiber jumpers, sets azimuth/downtilt, all outdoors in wind, heat and around legacy corroded hardware that differs site to site.

Rooftop or urban stealth-site antenna replacement: building rooftop, penthouse wall, sled/ballast mount or screened enclosure; equipment carried up via elevator/hatch, working around parapets, HVAC units, other carriers' gear and tight fall-protection constraints; antennas swapped on standoff mounts and jumpers re-terminated and weatherproofed.

Vehicle and mobile-radio antenna replacement: swapping whip/NMO/roof-mount antennas on police, fire, utility or service vehicles in a fleet garage or shop bay, including removing the old element, checking/reseating the coax connector under the headliner or in the trunk, and installing and testing the new antenna (VSWR check).

In-building / DAS and low-level antenna replacement: swapping ceiling- or wall-mounted DAS antennas, repeater or Wi-Fi/land-mobile antennas in an office building, stadium, tunnel or hospital, working from a ladder or scissor lift above ceiling tiles, disconnecting and re-mating coax connectors and re-securing the antenna.

Microwave/backhaul dish or small ancillary antenna replacement at height: removing a 2–6 ft dish or small omni/GPS antenna from a tower leg or standoff, mounting the replacement, and performing fine azimuth/elevation alignment to peak the received signal level against a far-end site.

Heavy broadcast or public-safety base antenna replacement: exchanging FM/TV antenna sections or a large collinear on a tall guyed tower or building mast, using gin pole or crane rigging, bolting heavy flanged sections and connecting rigid line/transmission line, often on a nighttime or short-outage schedule.

Indoor equipment shelter, broadcast transmitter room or carrier headend: bolting rack-mount radios, amplifiers, power plants and shelves into 19-inch racks, and bolting/anchoring racks and cable trays to the floor and walls in a climate-controlled, institution-controlled facility with standard equipment.

Vehicle installations in a fleet/upfit shop bay: bolting mobile radio mounts, control-head brackets, antenna mounts and equipment consoles into police, fire, ambulance and service vehicles - drilling/tapping brackets and fastening into varied vehicle interiors on a lift or in a bay.

tasks.label: Install, connect, or test underground or aboveground grounding systems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Greenfield macro cell site: install the underground grounding electrode system — trench ~30 in. around the compound, lay 2 AWG bare tinned copper counterpoise ring, drive 8–10 ft copper-clad ground rods at corners, exothermically weld (cadweld) all rod and conductor connections, bond tower legs, ice-bridge posts and fence, then backfill and compact. Raw graded dirt lot, weather and soil vary site to site.

Tower-mounted grounding: climb a 100–300 ft monopole/self-support/guyed tower, install coax or hybrid-cable grounding kits at top, mid-point and base, mount tower ground bars, run down-conductors on the leg, and bond to the ground ring. Work at height, in wind, around live RF and existing carrier cabling.

Ground-level equipment bonding in a fenced carrier compound: install/replace the master ground bar in the shelter or on the cabinet, run #6–#2 green insulated conductors from radios, racks, BBUs, surge suppressors, generator and AC panel to the bar, crimp two-hole compression lugs, apply antioxidant, torque bolts, label and verify continuity.

Rooftop, small-cell or in-building DAS site: bond antenna mounts, sleds, cable trays and coax to the building grounding electrode system or structural steel, install a ground bar in the telecom room, route bonding conductors through existing penetrations and tie into the building ground. Layout differs at every building.

Testing and audit of an existing grounding system: fall-of-potential or clamp-on ground resistance measurement with auxiliary probes set out 100+ ft, continuity/bond checks on ground bars, tower legs and coax kits, inspection after lightning or theft damage, plus photo documentation and a test report.

Mobile/base radio grounding: bond a two-way radio, antenna mount and power leads to vehicle chassis ground in a fleet shop or bond a dispatch/base-station rack to the facility ground bus, then verify low-resistance connections.

sources.title: The World's First Fully Autonomous Trenching Solution — Built Robotics

tasks.label: Check antenna positioning to ensure specified azimuths or mechanical tilts and adjust as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Macro cell site build/modification: tech climbs a 100–300 ft monopole or lattice tower, checks each sector panel antenna's azimuth against the RF design (GPS alignment tool or compass) and mechanical downtilt with an inclinometer, loosens the pipe-mount clamp bolts and downtilt strut, rotates/tilts the 40–70 lb antenna, re-torques and documents. Wind, ice, varied legacy mount hardware, work positioned in fall-arrest gear.

Rooftop/urban site: antennas on sled, parapet, or standoff pipe mounts on a building roof; magnetic compass unreliable near steel/HVAC so a GPS-based alignment tool is used; tech verifies azimuth and mechanical tilt per RFDS, adjusts clamps and tilt brackets, re-documents. Congested roof, cable trays, screening walls, varied per building.

Microwave/backhaul dish alignment: verify and fine-tune azimuth and elevation of a 2–6 ft dish on a tower or rooftop against the path design, adjust coarse/fine azimuth and elevation screws while watching received signal level, confirm main lobe (not sidelobe) and lock down.

Small cell, pole-mounted, or venue antennas: node antennas on utility/streetlight poles in public right-of-way or DAS/venue antennas on walls and ceilings; work from a bucket truck or ladder; check azimuth/tilt per design drawing and adjust brackets, often with traffic control and municipal constraints.

Audit-only sweep at an existing site (post-construction close-out, annual inspection, acquisition due diligence, or post-storm check): measure and document as-built azimuths, mechanical tilts, plumb and heights for every antenna against design records; deliverable is the verified as-built report, with any corrective work scheduled separately.

Corrective sweep after a report of degraded coverage or a storm: tech goes aloft, finds one or more antennas rotated or tilted out of spec (slipped clamp, wind-shifted mount), re-aims to the specified azimuth/tilt, re-torques hardware, and confirms with alignment tool readings.

sources.system: Fori Automation robotic wheel aligner with robotic toe-set gear heads
sources.title: End of Line Testing Systems - Wheel Aligners, Headlamp Aimers, Robotic Toe Set & Automated Tooling Changeover - Fori Automation
sources.claim: Fori Automation builds end-of-line robotic wheel alignment cells in which robots measure a suspension angle and then mechanically adjust it to specification by turning a tie rod with a nut runner or a cam bolt with a servo gear head, holding toe within ±0.03 degrees.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: setting vehicle wheel alignment angles at end of line. It is the same control loop as antenna aiming — measure an angular deviation from a specified value, then drive a threaded/clamped mechanical joint with a torque-controlled nutrunner until the angle is within tolerance and lock it — performed autonomously on unfixtured-but-presented workpieces in a purpose-built cell, at angular precision far tighter than the ±1–2° required for antenna azimuth/tilt.

sources.title: Boeing Dual Robotic Antenna Measurement System - ETS-Lindgren
sources.claim: Boeing operates a Dual Robotic Antenna Measurement System in which two commercial six-axis industrial robots position antennas through precise spherical, cylindrical, and planar geometries inside an RF-shielded anechoic chamber, replacing custom antenna positioners.

It shows robots handling and orienting real antennas to commanded azimuth/elevation angles with metrology-grade angular accuracy inside a purpose-built enclosed cell — the positioning-and-verification half of checking and setting an antenna's azimuth and tilt.

tasks.label: Transport equipment to work sites, using utility trucks and equipment trailers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Urban/suburban cell-site run: tech loads hand tools, test sets, jumpers, small antennas and parts into a pickup or utility truck at a carrier warehouse or home yard, drives 20-60 miles of city streets and highway in traffic and weather, parks in a lot, alley or parking garage at a rooftop or monopole site, then unloads and carries the gear to the equipment cabinet.

Rural/remote macro-tower run with an equipment trailer: hitch a cable-reel, generator or gear trailer at the yard, tow it on highway then several miles of unpaved, rutted, sometimes muddy or snowy private access road through locked gates and cattle guards, position the trailer inside the tower compound and unhitch.

Heavy/oversize haul: sector antennas, RRUs, equipment cabinets, battery strings or ice-bridge steel loaded on a flatbed or boom truck, chained and strapped for road transport, hauled to the site and offloaded by boom, crane or rough-terrain forklift at the pad.

Intra-facility transport on institution-controlled premises: moving radios, spares and test gear from a stockroom or staging yard to the work point inside a carrier switch center, broadcast plant campus, port, airport, hospital, military base or stadium, over maintained internal roads and corridors with badge-controlled access.

Emergency/rapid deployment: hauling a cell-on-wheels, portable repeater, or generator to a storm-damaged, wildfire or event site with debris, degraded or blocked roads, no site preparation, ad-hoc positioning and an urgent timeline.

tasks.label: Take site survey photos or photos of work performed, using digital cameras.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Site survey / audit photos of tower-mounted equipment on an operational macro cell tower (80–300 ft): antennas, mounts, RRUs, coax runs, mount space for a proposed colocation, RAD-center views and surroundings. Outdoor, as-found rural or suburban compound; layout differs site to site; weather and terrain vary.

As-built / close-out photo package documenting work just performed at height: each coax and jumper connector, weatherproofing, grounding kits, hoisting grips, torque/label marks, antenna serial plates — arm's-length shots from the climbing position, many partly occluded by mount pipes, antennas or radio shrouds, taken to a carrier's photo checklist.

Ground-level compound photos at a cell or broadcast site: tower base and foundation, cabinet and shelter exteriors, generator/fuel tank, ice bridge, ground ring/bar, meter and disconnect, fence, gate and access road, plus wide context shots of surroundings. Outdoor, gravel/vegetated compound, weather exposed.

Rooftop, small-cell or pole-node photos in an urban/suburban setting: antennas and cabinets on a crowded rooftop, a node on a streetlight or utility pole, associated cable trays and mounts — survey photos before work and exterior as-built photos after. Site taken as found, with traffic, pedestrians and mixed rooftop clutter.

Indoor photos inside a controlled building: equipment shelter or telecom/BTS room, broadcast transmitter building, headend, in-building DAS closet — racks, BBUs, cable trays, labeling, breaker panels, ceiling-mounted DAS antennas, documenting the installed work.

Photos of a two-way radio installation in a service or emergency vehicle at a fleet garage/shop: control head under the dash, radio body in the trunk/console, antenna mount and cable routing, before-and-after shots for the work order.

tasks.label: Climb towers to access components, using safety equipment, such as full-body harnesses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Climb a 100-250 ft monopole or self-support cell tower inside a fenced, tower-company-managed ground compound, ascending on step bolts/safety-climb cable in a full-body harness while carrying hand tools, rigging and hardware, to reach antenna/RRU mounting positions and work aloft (install or swap antennas, radios, jumpers, mounts).

Climb a tall lattice or guyed tower (250-1,000+ ft, broadcast or rural wireless) at a remote site reached by dirt road: long ascent, transfers around guy-wire and star-mount levels, rest stops and 100% tie-off, to reach transmission line, antenna or beacon components.

Unplanned/emergency climb for troubleshooting and repair: replace a failed obstruction light or photocell, re-seat a loose connector, repair weatherproofing or storm damage, often on short notice in wind, cold, heat or after dark, with the fault location unknown until the tech is aloft.

Rooftop or building-mounted site: hatch/fixed-ladder access to a penthouse or roof, then climb a short mast, parapet or sled mount in harness with anchorage/lifeline, weaving among HVAC units and other tenants' antennas, to service antennas and cabling.

Climb purely to inspect and document: routine structural/visual inspection, close-out or as-built audit - photographing and recording antennas, RRUs, mounts, cable routing, azimuth/tilt and hardware condition, with no equipment change made during the climb.

Climb a non-standard structure: water tank, stealth pole/flagpole/steeple, grain leg, silo, billboard or building-side mount, with irregular or missing climbing facilities and improvised anchorage, to reach concealed antennas and coax.
