tasks.label: Test equipment for overheating, using speed gauges and thermometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Post-repair heat-run/run test in an electric motor repair (rewind) shop: a rebuilt integral-horsepower AC motor is set on the shop test stand or coupled to a load, run up, and the technician takes frame, winding and bearing-housing temperatures with an IR/contact thermometer at intervals until thermal stabilization while checking shaft rpm with a tachometer against nameplate, then records temperature rise on the job card.

Routine temperature/overheating survey of running equipment on an industrial plant floor (in-house maintenance or a customer contract): technician walks a route past dozens of motors, pumps, fans, gearboxes and drives, shooting housing and bearing temperatures with an IR thermometer or thermal camera, spot-checking speeds, logging readings and flagging hot units for follow-up.

Bench test of a repaired power tool or small motor (drill, grinder, blower, appliance motor) in a shop: run no-load and under brief load on the bench, IR thermometer on the housing/field, tachometer or strobe for no-load rpm against the spec sheet, verify it does not run hot before returning it to the customer.

On-site troubleshooting of an overheating complaint on installed equipment inside a customer plant or commercial building: motor is in place, often cramped or elevated, running under its actual driven load; technician takes repeated contact and IR temperature readings over time, measures shaft/fan speed and slip with a tachometer, checks ventilation and ambient, and judges whether the machine is overloaded or failing.

Field service at unstructured sites — farm irrigation pump motors, well pumps, rooftop or attic HVAC blower motors, small shops and residences: access by ladder or crawl, variable weather and clutter, temperature and speed measurements taken with handheld gauges on whatever equipment is found there.

tasks.label: Reface, ream, and polish commutators and machine parts to specified tolerances, using machine tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In a motor repair shop, a DC motor or generator armature with brush-worn commutator is mounted between centers/chuck on a lathe or dedicated armature machine; the tech skims the commutator round and concentric, undercuts the mica slots, chamfers/deburrs the bar edges, and burnishes/polishes the surface to specified runout and finish, verified with dial indicator and micrometer.

Rotor/armature shaft repair in the shop: worn bearing journals and coupling fits are turned, ground (often after metal spray build-up), and hand-polished with abrasive cloth to a press/slip fit within a few ten-thousandths, checked with micrometer and dial indicator.

Sleeve-bearing and bushing work: boring, reaming, or honing bronze bushings and end-bracket bearing housings to size for shaft fit, plus refacing bracket rabbet fits on a lathe/mill, gauged with bore gauge and checked for concentricity.

Small universal-motor armatures from power tools and appliances (drill, saw, vacuum motors): commutator skimmed on a small armature lathe, mica undercut, edges deburred and surface polished, on batches of small, light rotors at a bench station.

Miscellaneous machine parts: refacing slip rings, dressing end brackets and mating faces, cleaning up keyways and shaft ends, deburring and buffing/polishing components on lathe, surface grinder, or pedestal buffer to drawing tolerance and finish.

Field/in-situ work at a customer plant: commutator or slip rings of an installed large motor/generator are stoned, ground, or polished in place (or a shaft journal machined with a portable in-situ machine) without removing the machine from its foundation, in confined access with the unit only partly disassembled.

tasks.label: Cut and form insulation, and insert insulation into armature, rotor, or stator slots.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Motor repair shop bench: random-wound three-phase AC stator, roughly 1-100 hp (IEC 80-250 frame), stripped and cleaned. Tech measures core stack length, cuts Nomex/DMD slot-cell material to length, creases/folds the cuffs, and seats a cell in each of ~24-48 semi-closed slots before rewinding.

Small armature/rotor work: universal-motor or DC power-tool armature (20-75 mm OD, 8-24 slots) or small wound rotor. Cut and form U-shaped slot liners from insulation stock and press one into each armature slot before winding; tight slot openings, thin paper.

Fractional-hp and specialty small motors in the shop (pump, fan, hood, compressor, servo, hermetic units): cut and crease cell insulation to short stack lengths, insert into stator slots, and cut matching phase separators and top sticks from the same sheet stock.

Large machine rewind on the shop floor: 200-3,000 hp form-wound or large random-wound stator, medium/high voltage, open slots, core several feet in diameter on stands. Cut ground-wall slot liners, side/center packing (glastic) and phase insulation to lengths taken off the old winding, form them, and place them in each slot.

Field/on-site work: replacing or patching slot insulation, packing and wedges in an installed motor or generator at a plant, mine, or mill - machine partly disassembled in place, awkward access, ambient dirt and no fixturing.

tasks.label: Assemble electrical parts such as alternators, generators, starting devices, and switches, following schematic drawings and using hand, machine, and power tools.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Auto-electric/remanufacturing shop bench: reassembling a rebuilt alternator or starter motor on a common model - pressing bearings onto the rotor shaft, seating the stator, installing rectifier bridge, regulator and brush holder, aligning drive- and slip-ring-end housings, running through-bolts to torque, then bench testing output. Repetitive across a handful of high-volume part numbers.

Electric motor repair shop: reassembling a fractional- to medium-horsepower industrial AC motor after rewind - pressing bearings, inserting the rotor into the stator, mounting end brackets and fan/shroud, dressing and connecting the winding leads in the terminal box per the connection diagram, torquing hardware, then no-load run test. Model and frame size vary job to job.

Shop bench/panel build area: assembling starting devices and switch assemblies - building up a magnetic starter or contactor (coil, armature, contact carrier, overload block), or mounting and wiring switches, terminal blocks and control components onto a mounting plate/DIN rail per a schematic, using crimpers, screwdrivers and torque tools, then continuity/hipot check.

Power tool / small motor service center: assembling the electrical guts of a tool or small universal motor - armature with commutator and bearings, field coils, brush holders, trigger switch and cord set into the housing per an exploded parts diagram, then run and leakage test.

Large machine bay: assembling a large industrial motor or generator end (hundreds of horsepower, crane-handled) - fitting rotor and exciter, sleeve or large anti-friction bearings, air baffles, custom shimming and air-gap checks, bolting end shields, landing leads on large terminal studs.

Field service at a customer site: assembling and mounting a starting device, switch, or generator control section on the plant floor, in a pump house, or on a skid, wiring it per schematic with hand and power tools in whatever space and access the site offers.

tasks.label: Solder, wrap, and coat wires to ensure proper insulation.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Motor rewind shop bench: after rewinding a fractional/integral-hp stator or armature, the repairer solders (or brazes) coil-lead-to-lead-wire connections, slides on insulating sleeving and half-laps electrical tape over each joint, then brushes or dips the connections and winding in insulating varnish before bake. Each unit is a different make/model; leads are hand-formed and positioned by eye.

Power tool / small appliance bench repair: resoldering field-coil, brush-holder, switch, cord and commutator lead connections on drills, saws, blowers and pumps; applying heat-shrink tubing or tape and occasionally sealant/lacquer over the joint, inside a cramped tool housing on a repair bench.

Large-machine coil work in a repair shop: half-lap mica/glass taping of form-wound coils, connection rings and brazed series connections on medium- and high-voltage motors and generators, followed by application of insulating resin/varnish (brush, dip or VPI) to the taped connections.

On-site field service at a customer's industrial or commercial facility: making up, soldering and insulating motor lead splices in a conduit/terminal box on an installed pump, fan or conveyor motor - kneeling or on a ladder, taping with rubber and vinyl tape and coating with insulating sealant, often in dirt, heat or limited access.

Field service at an uncontrolled site (private home, farm, rooftop, jobsite): soldering and insulating leads on a well pump, garage-door opener, HVAC blower or portable tool in place, with variable lighting, clutter and no fixed layout.

Field service at a customer's plant or commercial building: after lockout/tagout, rewire motor terminal connections on installed equipment, replace magnetic starters, contactors, disconnect switches, cords, plugs and control wiring, working from ladders or in tight machine spaces, then verify rotation and current draw.

Shop rework where the job is essentially installing a complete new, standardized wire set/harness into a repeatable enclosure or unit (e.g., rebuilt control panel or pump/genset skid of a known model), routing wires and landing them on terminal strips per a wiring diagram, then continuity testing.

Shop rework of a damaged, non-standard wiring harness or control panel on a machine, pump skid or generator set: trace and diagnose the fault, cut out and pull the damaged harness through the frame, fabricate and route replacements around existing structure, label and land wires, test.

Installing form-wound (taped, rigid) coils into the open slots of a medium-voltage stator core in the shop: laying bottom and top bars/coils in slots, packing and wedging, bracing and blocking end windings, then brazing series/phase connections.

On-site (in-situ) rewind at a customer plant or generating station: coils are made in the shop or supplied, but the stripping and rewinding of the core happens in place inside the machine housing, in a plant hall or nacelle with limited access.

tasks.label: Remove and replace defective parts such as coil leads, carbon brushes, and wires, using soldering equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Motor rewind/repair shop bench: on an industrial AC motor or stator whose leads are burnt or damaged, the repairer cuts out the defective lead wires, cleans the coil-end/terminal-block joints, joins and solders new leads, and sleeves them; the stator sits clamped on a bench or rack in a shop kept to a working standard.

Power tool / small universal-motor bench repair in a service shop: open the tool housing, pull worn carbon brushes, desolder their pigtails or terminals, fit new brushes, and resolder; also replace damaged cord or switch wiring. Wide mix of makes and models, dusty and worn used units, non-standard fastener layouts.

DC motor / armature bench repair: desolder defective coil leads from commutator risers or field-coil connections on a used armature clamped in a fixture, remove the defective lead, and solder in the replacement with a resistance soldering unit or heavy iron.

Motor control and accessory electrical repair at a shop bench: desolder and replace burnt wires, terminal lugs, and small components on motor control boards, starters, and switch assemblies, using soldering iron, desoldering braid/pump.

Field service inside a customer's plant or institutional facility: replace worn carbon brushes, brush-holder leads, and burnt wiring on a motor, generator, or elevator machine in place; cramped access inside the machine frame, portable soldering equipment, motor not removable.

On-site repair in an unstructured setting (construction site, farm, marine dock, customer premises): replace a tool's cord, brushes, or internal wires where the equipment sits, with a portable soldering iron and no bench or fixture.

Field service at a customer plant or facility: hammering out a dented cooling cover, guard, or terminal box, or straightening a bent bracket or conduit, on equipment still installed in place - awkward access, no bench or anvil, hand tools carried in the service van.

tasks.label: Repair and operate battery-charging equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On-site diagnosis and repair of a failed industrial battery charger in a customer's warehouse battery room: verify AC input at the disconnect, check fuses, contactors, SCR/rectifier stacks, transformer taps and control board with meter/scope, replace failed parts, re-terminate burned DC cables/connectors, verify charge profile and output under load.

Bench repair/refurbishment of chargers and charger assemblies in the repair shop: open the enclosure, trace the fault, do component-level board work (desolder/replace diodes, caps, relays), rewire harnesses, replace timers/controls, reassemble and load-test before returning the unit.

Routine operation of charging equipment in an industrial battery room or fleet depot: connect forklift batteries or electric equipment to the correct charger, select and start the right charge cycle, monitor progress/faults, disconnect and return the battery or vehicle to service.

Charging and cycle/capacity testing of batteries in the shop as part of service: place new, repaired or rebuilt batteries on charge, run equalize/boost cycles, perform discharge-capacity or load tests with test equipment, record results and pass/fail the unit.

Installing, replacing or commissioning battery-charging equipment at a facility: mount the charger, land the AC feed to a disconnect/panel, terminate DC leads and connectors, set voltage taps and charge profile for the battery type, commission and test.

Field service on charging equipment at unstructured sites: EV/utility-vehicle chargers in open parking lots, golf-course cart barns, farm or construction yards; troubleshoot in weather with no fixed layout, replace cables, connectors, boards or whole units.

tasks.label: Sharpen tools such as saws, picks, shovels, screwdrivers, and scoops, either manually or by using bench grinders and emery wheels.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repair-shop bench work: resharpening circular saw blades (carbide-tipped and steel), band/jig/reciprocating blades brought in with customers' power tools; worker checks tooth geometry, grinds face and top, avoids overheating, verifies cut quality before return.
Outdoor power-equipment service shop: sharpening chainsaw chains on a chain grinder, and grinding/balancing rotary mower blades and hedge-trimmer cutters during tune-up service.

Shop bench grinder / emery wheel work on small hand tools while servicing electric tools and motors: dressing screwdriver tips back to square, regrinding chisels, punches, scrapers and drill bits, dipping to keep temper, checking fit in fastener heads.

Shop grinding of heavy digging and material-handling tools brought in by contractors and municipalities: shovels, picks, mattocks, hoes, scoops, axes — restoring a bevel on a bench grinder or belt sander, deburring and wire-brushing before return.

Field/mobile service call at a customer jobsite, farm, or rental yard: sharpening shovels, picks, blades or bits on the spot with a portable grinder, file, or truck-mounted bench grinder amid clutter, weather, and other trades working nearby.

tasks.label: Test battery charges, and replace or recharge batteries as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Repair-shop bench: technician checks a customer's cordless power-tool battery pack (mixed brands/voltages) with a multimeter, load tester or charger diagnostics, decides whether the pack just needs a recharge or is failed, puts it on the correct charger or fits a replacement pack, and verifies the tool runs.

Repair-shop bench, cell-level work: open a pack or a device's battery compartment, test individual cells or backup batteries, unweld/replace weak cells or control-board backup batteries, reassemble, recharge and re-test capacity.

Shop service bay: larger equipment brought in (floor scrubber, generator, lift, golf cart, small engine unit) — load-test the starter/traction battery, check charger and charging circuit output, then recharge or swap in a new battery.

On-site at a customer's industrial or commercial facility: test batteries in installed or fleet equipment (UPS/emergency-light strings, battery-powered material-handling equipment, motor-control backup cells), then recharge or replace on the spot amid plant traffic.
On-site at an unstructured location (residence, farm, construction site, working out of a service truck): test tool/equipment batteries as found, in clutter and weather, and recharge or replace them.
